extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and students of dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on composing tragic drama (plot, character, and structural devices) following Aristotle's Poetics: principles for unity, magnitude, reversal/recognition, parts of tragedy, and the moral/status requirements of tragic protagonists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholeness of the plot (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole is that which has a beginning, a middle, and an end. A beginning is that which does not itself follow anything by causal necessity; an end is that which has nothing following it; a middle follows something and has something following it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-constructed plot must neither begin nor end at haphazard, but conform to these principles so the work forms a unified whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper magnitude (length)
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful object (or plot) must be of a certain magnitude; in a plot a certain length is necessary, and a length which can be easily embraced by the memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making the piece so short that its view is confused, or so long that the unity and sense of the whole are lost (e.g., impossibly long works). The proper magnitude allows the sequence of events, according to probability or necessity, to admit a change from bad fortune to good or vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (one action as the imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot, being an imitation of an action, must imitate one action and that a whole, the structural union of the parts being such that if any one of them is displaced or removed, the whole will be disjointed and disturbed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity of plot does not consist in unity of the hero; many events in one man's life cannot be reduced to a single action. Construct the plot around one coherent action rather than simply one character's life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic universality — represent the possible/probable
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the poet's work to relate what may happen—what is possible according to the law of probability or necessity—rather than merely what has happened; poetry tends to express the universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape events so they exemplify general types (how a person of a certain sort will act), not merely recount particular historical facts; credibility arises from probability/necessity, not mere reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility: use of names and traditional material
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets need not adhere rigidly to received legends; tragedies often use known names because what has happened is manifestly possible, but fictitious names or incidents may be used successfully if credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may invent or alter details of traditional myths to serve unity and probability; what matters is plausibility and the effect on the plot, not slavish fidelity to received stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic (epeisodic) plot
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'epeisodic' plot is one in which episodes or acts succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence; such plots are the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodic structure often arises from bad poets or pressure to make show-pieces (e.g., stretching for competitions). Ensure episodes follow by necessity or probability from what precedes to keep natural continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy aims to arouse pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is the imitation of a complete action and of events inspiring fear or pity. Such effect is best produced when the events come on us by surprise and, at the same time, follow as cause and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design incidents to surprise the audience while preserving causal plausibility; causes and effects heighten tragic wonder more than mere coincidence or spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex plots
rubrics_metrics.description: A Simple action: one and continuous, where the change of fortune takes place without Reversal of the Situation and without Recognition. A Complex action: one in which the change is accompanied by Reversal, or by Recognition, or by both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots (with peripeteia/anagnorisis) are superior because they produce stronger emotional effects when reversals/recognitions arise from the plot's internal structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of the Situation (peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite, subject to the rule of probability or necessity (e.g., the messenger meant to cheer Oedipus but produces the opposite effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage reversals so they are credible consequences of preceding events; reversal should feel necessary or probable within the story's logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune. The best form is coincident with a Reversal of the Situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognition to deepen emotional impact—especially powerful when combined with reversal (as in Oedipus). Recognition can be of persons, acts, or even trivial objects if tied to the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene of Suffering (pathos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Scene of Suffering is a destructive or painful action, such as death on the stage, bodily agony, wounds and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenes of suffering are a distinct part of tragic effect; include them when they naturally arise from the action and contribute to pity/fear, not merely as spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts of tragedy (prologue, episode, exode, choric parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The separate parts into which Tragedy is divided: Prologue (part that precedes the Parode), Episode (part between complete choric songs), Exode (part after which there is no choric song). Choric parts: Parode (the first undivided utterance of the Chorus), Stasimon (choric ode without anapaests or trochaic tetrameters), Commos (joint lamentation of Chorus and actors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange these parts with regard to their function and quantity; know their definitions and place them so they serve the unity and effect of the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate moral/status type of tragic protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune presented must not be the spectacle of a virtuous man brought from prosperity to adversity, nor of a bad man passing from adversity to prosperity, nor the downfall of the utter villain. The fitting subject is a man 'not eminently good and just, yet whose misfortune is brought about not by vice but by some error or frailty'—one highly renowned and prosperous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose protagonists of high status and reputation whose downfall stems from hamartia (error/frailty), so pity (for unmerited suffering) and fear (for the likeness to ourselves) can be evoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single vs double plot (unity of issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: A well constructed plot should be single in its issue rather than double; the change of fortune should be from good to bad rather than from bad to good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a single, unified catastrophic outcome that follows from the plot's logic; avoid contriving double-thread resolutions to pander to audience weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer inner-structural causes over spectacular monstrosities
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacle, but they may also result from the inner structure of the piece, which is the better way and indicates a superior poet. Those who employ spectacular means to create a sense of the monstrous are strangers to the purpose of Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on plot mechanics, reversal, recognition, and credible causality to produce tragic emotion rather than on mere visual shock or extraordinary spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances that elicit pity/fear (relationships and kinship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of arousing pity or fear must happen between persons who are friends, enemies, or indifferent; the most moving are those among friends or kin (e.g., brother killing brother, son killing father, mother killing son).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate tragic acts within close personal relationships (family, friends) to maximize pity/fear. Maintain or adapt traditional myths skilfully rather than breaking their framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of committing horrific deeds (knowledge/ignorance ranking)
rubrics_metrics.description: The action may be done consciously (with knowledge), done in ignorance, be about to act knowing then not act (shocking but not tragic), or be about to act in ignorance and discover the truth before acting. Aristotle ranks these possibilities and deems some better for tragic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the worst mode (being about to act knowing then not acting). Prefer outcomes where ignorance leads to later recognition or where a near-deed is averted by recognition—these produce stronger tragic impact; acting unknowingly then recognizing is also powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (êthos) considerations: goodness, fittingness, similarity/consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four considerations about characters (ἤθη) to be taken into account: first, how they will appear (goodness—if an action or speech makes character evident, it's 'good'); second, the fittingness or appropriateness of traits (e.g., bravery may not suit a woman); third, the similar/consistent (likeness to what is plausible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters morally plausible and consistent with their social role and gender/position; virtues and faults should fit the person and be manifest in word and deed so the audience believes their choices and misfortunes.
